title: The effect of vertical mixing on oxygen sequestration by refractory elements in the atmosphere of giant planets
byline: Simonetti; Paolo; Turrini; Diego; Schisano; Eugenio; Ivanovski; Stavro L; Politi; Romolo; Fonte; Sergio; Pacetti; Elenia; Molinari; Brogi; Matteo; Polychroni; D
html:
Abstract:The most widely used route to study the formation history of giant exoplanets is the C/O ratio, usually derived from H$_2$O, CO, CO$_2$ and CH$_4$. However, refractory elements can sequester a significant fraction of O, causing the observed C/O ratio to be overestimated with respect to the intrinsic one. Previous calculations of this bias relied on chemical equilibrium models. Here we quantify the impact of vertical mixing using the 1-D chemical kinetics code VULCAN, expanded with a Mg-Si-Fe network including the condensation and settling of enstatite, forsterite and metallic iron. We compute 168 models spanning equilibrium temperatures $T_{eq} \in$ [700, 1500] K, eddy diffusion coefficients $K_{zz} \in$ [$10^6$, $10^{10}$] cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$ and metallicities $Z \in$ [0.9, 7.2] $Z_\odot$, derived self-consistently from planet formation simulations. We find that vertical transport causes magnesium silicates to destabilize already at $T_{eq} \sim 900$ K regardless of metallicity, releasing oxygen to H$_2$O and to minor gas-phase carriers such as SiO and Mg(OH)$_2$. Therefore, while equilibrium models predict a nearly constant C/O overestimation up to 1100-1300 K, in disequilibrium it drops sharply between 900 and 1200 K. In this transitional range the C/O overestimation is controlled by $K_{zz}$ and is partially degenerate with metallicity, while outside it is robust against both mixing intensity and the probed atmospheric layer, ranging from 14.5-23\% at 700 K to 4.5-7\% at 1500 K. Metallic iron condensation prevents Fe from sequestering oxygen, lowering the overestimation by about one third with respect to previous estimates. Finally, CH$_4$, CO$_2$ and the CH$_4$/CO ratio are most sensitive to $K_{zz}$ in the transitional range, and can provide a constraint on vertical mixing.
